title: Reading Maps and Giving Directions
objectives: Use directional vocabulary including north, south, east, west, left, right, and block
Give step-by-step spoken and written directions between two locations
Interpret a simple street map and identify landmarks
Ask for clarification when directions are unclear or confusing

reading_passage.title: How Landmarks Help Us Navigate
reading_passage.text:
Before GPS became common, people relied heavily on landmarks — recognizable buildings, intersections, or natural features — to give and receive directions. Even today, directions that include landmarks are often clearer than those using only street names and compass points. Saying 'turn left at the red mosque' is more immediately useful to someone unfamiliar with an area than 'turn west on NE Glisan Street.'

Researchers have found that people process landmark-based directions more quickly and make fewer wrong turns than when following address-only instructions. This is partly because landmarks engage visual memory — when you have seen a building or a park before, you can recognize it even under stress.

For newcomers navigating an unfamiliar city, the challenge is that landmarks are only helpful once you know them. In Portland, new residents often learn the grid system first: streets running east to west are called 'streets,' while those running north to south are called 'avenues.' The city is divided into quadrants — NE, NW, SE, and SW — which helps narrow down locations significantly.

Combining both systems is the most effective strategy. For example, a skilled local might say, 'Take the 72 bus south to Division Street — you'll see the big Fred Meyer on the corner. Get off there and walk east two blocks. The clinic is just past the laundromat, on your right.' This kind of direction mixes route numbers, compass points, specific distances, and a visual landmark — giving the listener multiple ways to confirm they are on the right path.
reading_passage.source: Adapted from an urban navigation study published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology, 2022

glossary.meaning: an easily recognized building, sign, or feature used as a reference point for navigation
the four main directions: north, south, east, and west
a city layout where streets run in straight lines forming a pattern of squares
one of four sections created when a city is divided by north-south and east-west lines
to find your way or plan a route from one place to another

comprehension.question: According to the passage, what do researchers say about landmark-based directions?
comprehension.answer: Researchers found that people process landmark-based directions more quickly and make fewer wrong turns compared to address-only instructions.

comprehension.question: What does the author imply when they say landmarks 'engage visual memory'?
comprehension.answer: The author implies that because we remember things we have seen visually, landmarks we recognize help us navigate even when we are stressed or distracted.

comprehension.question: What does the word 'quadrant' mean in paragraph three?
comprehension.answer: One of four sections that a city is divided into — in Portland, these are NE, NW, SE, and SW.

comprehension.question: Why does the author include the example direction at the end of the passage ('Take the 72 bus south...')?
comprehension.answer: To demonstrate how combining different types of information — route numbers, compass points, distances, and landmarks — makes directions easier to follow.

language_focus.title: Imperative Sentences for Giving Directions
language_focus.explanation: When giving directions, we use imperative sentences — commands that start directly with a verb and have no stated subject. The implied subject is 'you.' This makes directions sound direct and clear. We often combine imperatives with prepositions of location (at, past, along, onto) and distance phrases (two blocks, half a mile).

examples.sentence: Turn left at the traffic light, then continue straight for two blocks.
examples.note: Both 'turn' and 'continue' are imperatives — no subject is needed because we are clearly talking to the listener.

examples.sentence: Walk past the library, and you will see the clinic on your right.
examples.note: The second clause ('you will see') adds a result or confirmation, helping the listener know they are on track.

practice.sentence: Rewrite as an imperative direction: 'You need to go north on 82nd Avenue for three blocks.'
practice.answer: Go north on 82nd Avenue for three blocks.

practice.sentence: Complete this direction: '___ right on Division Street and ___ straight until you reach the park.'
practice.answer: Turn right on Division Street and go/walk straight until you reach the park.

practice.sentence: Which is a correctly formed direction? A) You should turning left here. B) Turn left here.
practice.answer: B) 'Turn left here.' is the correct imperative form. Option A incorrectly combines 'should' with a gerund.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: A well-known or easily noticed building or feature used to help people find their way
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: Directions that include landmarks are often clearer than those using only street names and compass points.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: To successfully find your way through or around an unfamiliar place
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: For newcomers navigating an unfamiliar city, the challenge is that landmarks are only helpful once you know them.

vocabulary_in_context.definition: One of four sections that a city or area is divided into, based on a central point
vocabulary_in_context.example_sentence: The city is divided into quadrants — NE, NW, SE, and SW — which helps narrow down locations significantly.

speaking_task.context: A new neighbour has just moved to your area and does not know the neighbourhood at all. They need to get from your building to the nearest grocery store.
speaking_task.prompt: Give your neighbour clear spoken directions from your home to a nearby grocery store or market. Include at least one landmark they should look for, compass directions or left/right instructions, and a distance estimate. Your directions should be detailed enough that they can follow them without getting lost.
useful_language: Go straight along... until you reach...
Turn left/right at the corner of... and...
You will see a [landmark] on your left/right — that is how you know you are going the right way.
speaking_task.model_answer: Exit the building and turn right. Walk south along 82nd Avenue for about three blocks. You will pass a laundromat on your left — keep going past it. When you reach Division Street, turn right and walk west for one block. You will see a large Fred Meyer store on the corner — you cannot miss it. That is the grocery store. The whole walk takes about ten minutes.

writing_workshop.model_text: To get from the community center to the public library, start by walking east on Burnside Street for two blocks. Turn left at the traffic light — you will see a small park on your right. Continue north for one block. The library is the large red-brick building on the left side of the street, just past the coffee shop. The walk takes about eight minutes.
writing_workshop.model_analysis: Notice how the writer uses imperative verbs throughout (walk, turn, continue), provides a landmark for confirmation, and ends with a practical detail about travel time.
writing_workshop.task: Write directions from your home or school to a nearby place (a bus stop, a park, a store, or a clinic). Use imperative verbs, at least one landmark, and include how long the journey takes.
success_criteria: Use at least four imperative verbs (turn, walk, go, continue, pass, cross)
Include at least one landmark to help the reader confirm they are going the right way
Mention how long the walk takes or the approximate distance

quiz.question: According to the passage, what makes landmark-based directions easier to follow?
options: They are shorter and use fewer words
They engage visual memory, making recognition easier under stress
They only require knowing compass directions
They were invented specifically for newcomers to the city
quiz.explanation: The passage explains that landmarks 'engage visual memory' — because we remember things we have seen, recognizable buildings help us navigate even when we are stressed.

quiz.question: In Portland's grid system, what is the difference between a 'street' and an 'avenue'?
options: Streets are wider than avenues
Streets run east to west; avenues run north to south
Avenues run east to west; streets run north to south
There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
quiz.explanation: The passage states: 'streets running east to west are called streets, while those running north to south are called avenues.'

quiz.question: Which sentence is a correctly formed imperative direction?
options: You are turning left at the school.
Please to turn left at the school.
Turn left at the school.
Turning left at the school.
quiz.explanation: Imperative sentences begin with the base verb directly — no subject, no auxiliary, no '-ing' form.

quiz.question: What does the author suggest is the most effective navigation strategy?
options: Using only GPS and avoiding verbal directions
Memorising all street names in the city
Combining route numbers, compass points, distances, and landmarks
Using only landmarks and avoiding street names
quiz.explanation: The final paragraph describes an effective direction that mixes 'route numbers, compass points, specific distances, and a visual landmark — giving the listener multiple ways to confirm they are on the right path.'

listening_exercises.transcript: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the public library? Sure. Go straight on this street for two blocks. Then turn left at the traffic light. The library is on your right, across from the bank. You can't miss it — it's a big brick building with a blue sign. It's about a ten-minute walk from here.
listening_exercises.question: Where is the library?
options: Next to the traffic light
On the right, across from the bank
Two blocks behind the bank
On the left, next to a school

listening_exercises.transcript: Map apps on your phone can give you directions for walking, driving, or taking the bus. Type the address, then choose how you want to travel. The app shows the fastest route and how long it will take. If you don't have internet, you can download the map of your city before you leave home. That way the map still works without a connection.
listening_exercises.question: What can you do if you won't have internet?
options: Buy a paper map only
Download the city map before leaving
Ask the app for a transfer
Turn off your phone
